defs_parts: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the book text: the course text uses and explains the term.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a made-up run with a fixed seed, so it comes out the same every time.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: A measure is a stand-in for what you want, not the want itself.
Skepticism is a method, a set of moves that leave something to inspect.
The artifact is the output, the world is what it should describe.
In AI deployment, producing is cheap and verifying is costly.
The supervisory capacities belong to a human, and someone must own the decision.
Fluent is not correct, so write the failure condition before reading.

bookends.command: Quiz me on the skeptic's toolkit. Give me one short case at a time about an AI system. I must name the exact term, choosing from measure versus want, gap from the start, gap that opens later, Cartesian doubt, falsifiability, rhetorical claim, artifact versus world, plausibility auditing, interpretive judgment and fluency trap, and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold the answer until I reply, then grade me.

beats.narration_text: The same model twice, in a simulated run. Distribution shift means the world after deployment no longer resembles the training data. Before, confidence and accuracy are both eighty-four percent. After, the model says eighty-nine percent and is right sixty-six.
